If there are good sons or good daughters who hear these names of the Buddhas and the names of these sutras, all such good sons and good daughters shall be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas together, and they shall all attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.”
The commentary states:
This is the second general explanation.
"Virtuous sons and virtuous daughters" refers to those who are the objects of protection.
Those who hear the name of this Amitābha Buddha and hear the names of the Buddhas of the six directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are able to be protected and remembered by them.
These good sons and good daughters, all being protected and remembered by all the Buddhas, attain true protection and mindfulness.

Any man or woman who upholds this sutra and the names of the Buddhas, having heard the various Buddhas and Śākyamuni Buddha preach this Sutra on Cultivating the Pure Land, will only then be able to be born in the Pure Land; for this very sutra is that which all Buddhas protect, clarify, and cause one to remember and keep in mind.

Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*: "An" means "without," "uttara" means "above," "sam" means "right," "yak" means "equal," "saṃ" means "right," and "bodhi" means "awakening. Thus, it is the Unsurpassed, Right, Equal, and Perfect Awakening.
Question:
"Is it that by merely recollecting Amitābha Buddha one immediately attains non-retrogression, or are there further expedient means? Answer:

"Merely reciting the name and paying homage is not enough; one should also, with a sincere mind, perform repentance, entreaty, sympathetic joy, dedication, and the making of vows before all Buddhas. Through repentance, one transforms determinate karma; like a wish-fulfilling jewel, one obtains what is desired according to one's vows and attains non-retrogression."
"Because they are protected and sustained by all the Buddhas, they shall attain non-retrogression in their resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
The Sūtra says:
"Therefore, Śāriputra!"
"You all should believe and accept my words, as well as what has been spoken by all the Buddhas.
Commentary:
This is the third exhortation to conclude.
The phrase "for this reason" is a term used to conclude what has preceded.
The expression "all should be equal" is an exhortation.
You all should believe what I have said above, as well as the words of the Buddhas of the six directions.
The Sūtra says:
“Śāriputra! If there are those who have already made a vow, are now making a vow, or will make a vow, desiring to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha.”
The commentary states:
From this point downward, the fourth section concerns the generation of the vow.
This text is divided into four parts:
First, the arousal of the mind for rebirth;
second, the manifestation of its supreme benefits;
third, the stationing within the three periods of time.
Fourth, the exhortation to be born in that land.
This is the first [section].
Those who have already made the vow belong to the past; those who are now making the vow belong to the present; and those who shall make the vow belong to the future.
"Desire" refers to aspiration.
"Birth" refers to that which is conventionally designated as the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
As the Sūtra says:
"These people shall all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Commentary:
The second [section] clarifies their superior benefits.

Because of the power of reciting the Buddha’s name and making vows, on the one hand, that Buddha provides secret empowerment, and on the other, this Buddha offers hidden protection; thus, the mind seeking the Way does not regress and the resolve to be born [in the Pure Land] does not waver, which is why it is called "non-retrogression."

Those who have already made the vow and attained non-retrogression will now, by making the vow, attain non-retrogression in the present; those who shall make the vow in the future shall likewise attain the stage of non-retrogression.
The Sūtra says:
"In that land, those who have already been born, those who are being born now, or those who will be born.
The Commentary says:
The third stage abides throughout the three periods of time.
Those who have already made their vows belong to the past and have already been born.
Those who are making their vows now belong to the present and are being born at this very moment.
Regarding those who make vows for the future, they make vows for birth in the future of the future.
As the Sūtra says:
"Therefore, Śāriputra!"
"Good sons and good daughters, those who possess faith should make a vow to be born in that land.
The commentary states:
This is the fourth exhortation to be born in that land.
If one possesses deep and profound faith and has but slight afflictions, knowing that the Great Awakened One speaks with sincerity and that one will obtain a noble vow, then one should go.
As the Sūtra says:
"Śāriputra!..."
"Just as I now praise the inconceivable merit of all Buddhas, so too do those Buddhas proclaim my own inconceivable merit."
The commentary states:
Regarding the fifth section, the praise of that Honored One is universally declared to be marvelous.
This passage consists of four segments:
First, praising his inconceivable merit;
second, extolling his transformative activities in a defiled world;
third, marveling at his attainment of Buddhahood.
Fourth, the teaching of the Dharma is profound and subtle;
this passage is the beginning [of that].
I praise the Buddhas of the six directions for being able to speak words of truth for the sake of sentient beings, so that sentient beings have no doubts or delusions in their minds because of this.
Furthermore, as the Tathāgata Amitābha compassionately receives and guides us, we especially praise that Buddha, and that Buddha in turn praises us.
As the Sūtra says:

"And he spoke these words: 'Śākyamuni Buddha is able to perform a most difficult and rare feat; he is able, within the five turbidities of this Sahā world—the turbidity of the kalpa, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of life—to [attain enlightenment] amidst such an evil world.'"
The commentary states:
The second section praises the transformative practice in a defiled age.
The words "and he spoke thus" are the narration of the compilers.
Śākyamuni is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "Capable Benevolent One" (Néngrén). Muni is translated as "Silent Sage.
The circumstances regarding his acquisition of this clan name are explained elsewhere.
What is called an extremely difficult and rare feat refers precisely to the act of teaching and transforming sentient beings while enduring suffering.
Regarding "one who is able [to act] in the Sahā world": *Sahā* is the Sanskrit term, which here means "Endurance," because it is capable of enduring the occurrence of suffering and affliction.
Regarding the "five turbidities of the evil world," they are briefly explained by way of five sections:
first, the explanation of the names.
2. Establishing the essential nature; 3. Antidotes;
4. Abolishing and establishing.
V. Mutual Inclusion.

First, regarding the explanation of the names: "turbidity" (*āvilatā*) has the meaning of dregs and filth. Just as food that is dreggy, foul, inferior, and defiling is called turbid, so too are these [defilements] termed turbidities.

The meaning of this statement is that during the period of the increase of the kalpa, the three calamities gradually diminish, afflictions become increasingly attenuated, sentient beings incline toward the wholesome, wrong views gradually fade away, and the life-faculty becomes progressively longer, moving steadily toward excellence.
That which is already excellent, superior, and delightful is called "purity. If sentient beings were free from suffering, transformation-buddhas would not appear in the world.

Transformation-buddhas invariably appear when the kalpa is in decline; as the three minor calamities gradually arise, afflictions become increasingly thick. Sentient beings turn toward evil, defiled views gradually increase, their life-faculties grow shorter, and they progressively become inferior. Because these lower evils are loathsome, they are designated by the name "turbidity" (kaṣāya).
The fifth is "number," which is an explanatory compound (tatpuruṣa) based on a number.
Next, when viewed in relation to their specific names, they are all possessive compounds (karmadhāraya).
Alternatively, when using a specific term to distinguish it from the general, they are also locative-possessive compounds (bahuvrīhi).
2. Regarding the identification of its essence, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The people of the present age are for the most part short-lived; even the longest lifespan is one hundred years—this is called the defilement of life (*āyuḥ-kāṣāya*)."

This [life-faculty] has as its essence the specific functional capacity induced by karma, which consists of the seeds of names and words within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); because the power of wholesome karma is weak, the life-faculty gradually shortens, as it is brought about by the karma of taking life.

If sentient beings do not recognize their parents, nor recognize śramaṇas, kinsmen, or elders; if they do not cultivate righteous principles, nor feel dread or fear regarding the retribution of evil karma in this world and the next; if they do not practice generosity or perform meritorious deeds, nor cultivate the rules of purity or maintain the prohibitive precepts—this is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

Although the eighth consciousness is called "sentient being" (*sattva*), it is here stated that because of proximity to adverse external conditions, the provisional entity consisting of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) commits evil and lacks goodness; this is termed the "turbidity of sentient beings" (*sattva-kaṣāya*). Its nature is thus a combination of the eighth consciousness and the [other] five [aggregates].

If these sentient beings increase in unrighteous greed, or bestow swords and blades, or grant weapons; if they engage in litigation, strife, conflict, flattery, and falsehood; and if they embrace false teachings and other evil, unwholesome dharmas—this is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).

Excluding the five views (*pañcadṛṣṭi*), all remaining afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) constitute the essence of the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśakaṣāya*). It is not through unlawful greed, the sword of wisdom, and so forth, that one commits acts of killing; rather, it is because of unlawful greed and strife that one merely discards the sword and spear, yet ends up engaging in them. This extends to all other evil and unwholesome dharmas, which collectively encompass every affliction and secondary affliction. Because their nature is habitually practiced and they are drawn forth by encountering adverse objects, these afflictions become particularly heavy.

If, in this present age, the True Dharma is decaying and vanishing, while the Semblance Dharma gradually arises and false teachings increasingly emerge, this is called the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
This has the five views as its essential nature; it frequently draws near to the evil views of non-Buddhists and arises repeatedly.
When the kalpa of famine arises, the kalpa of disease arises, or the kalpa of weapons arises, these are called the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

This has the four objects of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) as its essence, or it may extend to all five aggregates; however, its essence remains the time of non-concomitance (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), because it is established based upon the four or five aggregates. As afflictions increase and evil karma becomes even more heavy, one invites evil fruits, and thus the three calamities (*trividha-vyasanāni*) eventually arise.
Third, regarding the remedies (*pratipakṣa*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* establishes the four *siddhāntas*, which constitute its fundamental tenets: first, the worldly *siddhānta*;
second, the *siddhānta* for the benefit of persons; [third, the *siddhānta* of ultimate truth; fourth, the *siddhānta* of therapeutic treatment].
Third, the therapeutic standpoint (pratipakṣa-siddhānta);
fourth, the standpoint of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya-siddhānta).
The defilement of the eon (kalpa-kaṣāya) and the defilement of sentient beings (sattva-kaṣāya) are treated by means of the worldly standpoint (loka-siddhānta).
The vessel-world and the world of sentient beings are entirely illusory; by cultivating the path with revulsion and fear toward them, one is forever liberated from them.
The impurity of lifespan is treated through the *puruṣa-saṃvṛti-satya* (the standpoint of individual human beings).

One should know that human beings obtain their existence through virtuous karma; by practicing and upholding the pure precepts, such as refraining from killing, their lifespan is naturally prolonged. Alternatively, for those of the three vehicles, one may preach the fruit of nirvana according to each respective vehicle, thereby eliminating the turbidity of life inherent within birth and death.
The turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) and the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) are treated by the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the therapeutic standpoint),
because one practices the appropriate path of counteraction so that they do not arise.
Since the five turbidities are destroyed by means of the three *siddhāntas*, one enters the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and realizes the true doctrine.
4. Regarding the establishment [of the number]: Why are there established as only five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya), neither more nor less?
Answer:
Sentient beings are of two kinds:
First, those of evil conduct, namely laypeople in white robes;

second, those of wrong conduct, namely renunciants and non-Buddhists. When laypeople lack wisdom and their afflictions increase, it is termed the *kleśa-kaṣāya* (affliction turbidity); when non-Buddhists engage in erroneous understanding and reckless seeking, it is established as the *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya* (view turbidity).
Furthermore, all dull delusions are termed the *kleśa-kaṣāya*, while all other sharp delusions are termed the *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*.

When these two causes attain their corresponding effects, they differ in terms of being distinct or combined; thus, they are further divided into two turbidities (*kaṣāya*). Combining the two internal effects is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), because they are evil beings;
combining the two external effects is collectively termed the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), because they are evil vessels.
A *kalpa* refers to a period of time; since time has no distinct temporal parts other than what is established by relying on phenomena, it is called the "impurity of the kalpa" (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
Its essence consists of the "vessel world" (*bhājana-loka*) being corrupt.
Although these corrupt sentient beings and external fruits are mentioned collectively, the specific results of these two impurities have not yet been distinguished.

Why is this? Because the essence of the primary evil fruits is now manifested as the root, the "impurity of life" (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*) is established; alternatively, internal evil fruits are termed the "impurity of life," while external evil fruits are termed the "impurity of the eon" (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
From whom do these evil causes and effects arise? They arise from evil sentient beings;
therefore, it is called the *sattva-kaṣāya* (degeneration of sentient beings).
Because these five degenerations are characterized by their predominant activity, and because one wishes to engender revulsion [toward cyclic existence], only these five are specifically mentioned.
Regarding the fivefold inclusion, the *Sāṭhāgata-nirgrantha-sūtra* states that twelve turbidities are established:
first, the manifestation of the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*);
second, the manifestation of the turbidity of the time (*kāla-kaṣāya*).
3. Manifesting the defilement of sentient beings;
4. Manifesting the defilement of afflictions;
5. Manifesting the defilement of lifespan;
Sixth, the defilement of manifesting the distinctions among the three vehicles;
seventh, the defilement of manifesting impure buddha-fields;
eighth, the defilement of sentient beings who are difficult to transform.
Nine, manifesting the teaching on the turbidity of various afflictions;
ten, manifesting the turbidity of the confusion of external paths;
eleven, manifesting the turbidity of Māra.
Twelfth, the manifestation of the turbidity of Māra’s activities:

the kalpa-turbidity and its time constitute the *kalpa-kaṣāya*; sentient beings and those difficult to transform constitute the *sattva-kaṣāya*; afflictions and the teaching of various afflictions constitute the *kleśa-kaṣāya*; lifespan constitutes the *āyuṣka-kaṣāya*; and the confusion of external paths constitutes the *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*. These eight are the five turbidities.
The remaining four types—namely, the distinctions among the three vehicles, impure lands, Māras, and the deeds of Māras—are not subsumed under the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*).
This is because the five turbidities refer primarily to the actual defilements;
whereas the twelve turbidities encompass both that which can transform and that which can obstruct, as they are manifested by the Buddha.
Question:
"For what reason was Śākyamuni born when the human lifespan was one hundred years, while Maitreya will appear when it is eighty thousand years? Answer:
"Because each [Buddha] acts according to their original vow, the timing of their appearance differs.
The Sūtra says:
"They attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The commentary states:
The third section expresses amazement at attaining Buddhahood.

Because this realm consists solely of defiled and evil beings, it is not worth judging as either right or wrong; that one realizes Bodhi therein is like a lotus growing within fire, and that one attains liberation is like a candle emerging from ice.
The Sūtra says:
"For the sake of all sentient beings, he expounds this Dharma which is difficult for the entire world to believe.
The Praise says:
The fourth teaching concerns the profound and mysterious Dharma that is difficult to believe.

Simply by reciting this scripture for a single day, or through ten moments of mindfulness with diligent sincerity, one transcends the defilements of the five turbidities and ascends to the pure realm of the first stage (*bhūmi*). Is this not indeed difficult to believe?
The fifth section above concludes with all those venerable ones offering praise, saying: "How marvelous!
The Sūtra states:
“Śāriputra! You should know that I perform this difficult task in the evil world of the five turbidities.
Commentary:
The sixth section below, in which our Buddha recounts what he alone has performed with difficulty,
is divided into four parts:
first, an account of the difficulty of practicing the conduct;
2. An account of how the fruit is difficult to realize;
3. An account of how the Dharma is difficult to believe;
4. A summary of its extreme difficulty.
This is the first point.

As for those who perform such difficult deeds, they cultivate the myriad practices throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, sacrifice their bodies and lives to pursue Bodhi, and renounce their kingdoms and cities for the sake of the masses; only then do they achieve Perfect Enlightenment—how could this not be a difficult task!
The Sūtra says:
"He attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Commentary says:
This second point describes the difficulty of realizing the fruit.
As explained above, the meaning of the text may be understood.
The Sūtra says:
"To preach this dharma difficult to believe for the sake of all the world.
The commentary states:
This third [section] describes the difficulty of believing the dharma.
The Sūtra says:
"This is exceedingly difficult.
The Commentary says:
This fourth section provides a summary of the extreme difficulty, concluding the three preceding matters.
The explanation of the *zhengzongfen* (the main body of the teaching) is hereby completed.
The Sūtra says:

“When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Śāriputra and all the bhikṣus, as well as all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and others—having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced, accepted it with faith, prostrated, and departed.”
The commentary states:
The third section, the *pariṇāmanā* (concluding) division, consists of four parts:
first, the completion of the discourse on the sutra;
Second, the conclusion of the conditions for hearing the Dharma;
third, rejoicing upon hearing the Dharma;
fourth, withdrawing and taking leave of the Buddha to depart—these four sections are chanted as one.
"When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra" refers to the conclusion of the first discourse;

the subsequent phrases, including "Śāriputra and the bhikṣus, along with all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and others—heard what the Buddha had spoken," mark the end of the second section concerning the conditions for hearing the Dharma.
What is called the "world" refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), for it is subject to destruction.
Regarding "gods and humans": "gods" refers to the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
As for the term "god" (*deva*), they are so named because they are radiant, pure, and possess mastery.
"Human" refers to the human realm; it is called "human" (nara) in the sense of having much patience (*kṣānti*).
Asuras are here translated as "non-gods" (*a-deva*); just as a person who lacks benevolence is called a "non-person," so too is an asura.

"Rejoicing with faith and acceptance" refers to the third stage of hearing the Dharma with joyful exultation: "joy" (*huan*) means the countenance relaxes, while "delight" (*xi*) means the spirit is pleased; hence it is called "rejoicing" (*huānxī*), which is the feeling of joy associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

This sutra contains the sublime essence of the Three Vehicles and the vital pivot of all sages; it is the great source for transcending birth and death and the swift path to realizing the true and eternal. To obtain this path and hear its complete and perfect teachings—how could one not rejoice!
Therefore, it says "rejoicing.
